studies.Title: Inverse associations between plasma lycopene and other carotenoids and prostate cancer.
studies.Reference: Inverse associations between plasma lycopene and other carotenoids and prostate cancer.
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
studies.Population: Patients with prostate cancer and cancer-free controls

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: The study included 65 patients with prostate cancer and 132 cancer-free controls
extraction_supporting_text.cases: The study included 65 patients with prostate cancer and 132 cancer-free controls; all of them were interviewed using a standard epidemiological questionnaire at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center from 1993 to 1997.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: After adjusting for age, race, years of education, daily caloric intake, pack-years of smoking, alcohol consumption, and family history of prostate cancer, significantly inverse associations with prostate cancer were observed with plasma concentrations of the following carotenoids: lycopene [odds ratio (OR), 0.17; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.04-0.78; P for trend, 0.0052] and zeaxanthin (OR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.06-0.83; P for trend, 0.0028) when comparing highest with lowest quartiles.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: After adjusting for age, race, years of education, daily caloric intake, pack-years of smoking, alcohol consumption, and family history of prostate cancer, significantly inverse associations with prostate cancer were observed with plasma concentrations of the following carotenoids: lycopene [odds ratio (OR), 0.17; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.04-0.78; P for trend, 0.0052] and zeaxanthin (OR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.06-0.83; P for trend, 0.0028) when comparing highest with lowest quartiles.
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: when comparing highest with lowest quartiles
extraction_supporting_text.location: at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_measurement: Plasma levels of carotenoids, retinol, and tocopherols were measured by high performance liquid chromatography.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an effect size of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.46–1.21), indicating no statistically significant association between zeaxanthin and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 64.08%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
